snapshots.name: The State of Nature
snapshots.subtitle: Life without a common power
snapshots.body: The condition Hobbes describes in Chapter XIII: men roughly equal in strength and wits, competing for the same scarce goods with no common power to keep them in awe. Without government, Hobbes argues, this equality produces not peace but a war of every man against every man, and life becomes "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short."

snapshots.name: War of Every Man Against Every Man
snapshots.subtitle: The condition of nature, defined
snapshots.body: Hobbes's technical name for the state of nature in its full consequence: not constant fighting, but a known disposition to fight with no security against it, in which nothing can be unjust because right and wrong have no place where there is no common power.

snapshots.name: The Covenant (Social Contract)
snapshots.subtitle: How the commonwealth is made
snapshots.body: The mutual transferring of right described in Chapter XVIII: each man authorizing one man or assembly to bear the person of them all, on condition every other man does the same, so that the many become united in one person by covenant of every man with every man.

snapshots.name: Leviathan, the Mortal God
snapshots.subtitle: The book's namesake
snapshots.body: Hobbes's name for the artificial man created by the covenant: the commonwealth itself, which he calls "that great LEVIATHAN, or rather (to speake more reverently) of that Mortall God," to which men owe their peace and defence under the immortal God.

snapshots.name: The Sovereign
snapshots.subtitle: Rights by institution
snapshots.body: The man or assembly in whom the covenanting multitude vests its united will, described in Chapter XVIII as holding rights — including judging opinions, making law, and commanding war and peace — that cannot be forfeited or divided without dissolving the commonwealth itself.

snapshots.name: The Fool
snapshots.subtitle: Who denies justice pays
snapshots.body: The figure Hobbes answers in Chapter XV: the fool who has said in his heart that there is no such thing as justice, and that breaking covenants is reasonable whenever it serves one's own preservation. Hobbes argues the fool is simply wrong about where his own interest lies.

snapshots.name: Aristotle
snapshots.subtitle: The political doctrine Hobbes rejects
snapshots.body: Repeatedly cited and argued against, especially in Chapter XVI, where Hobbes rejects Aristotle's claim in the Politics that some men are by nature more worthy to command and others, being naturally less rational, to serve — a doctrine Hobbes says has no place in the natural equality of men.

snapshots.name: Cardinal Bellarmine
snapshots.subtitle: Hobbes's target on papal power
snapshots.body: The Catholic theologian whose arguments for the temporal power of the pope over civil sovereigns Hobbes spends much of Chapter XLII refuting at length, treating him as the ablest and most dangerous defender of a divided sovereignty between church and state.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.subtitle: Cited on eloquence and personation
snapshots.body: The Roman orator and statesman Hobbes cites several times, including for the idea of "bearing a person" (Cicero's "I sustain three persons") that Hobbes builds on in his account of representation, and as an authority whose name alone some men mistake for proof.

snapshots.name: Julius Caesar
snapshots.subtitle: Example of ambition and its end
snapshots.body: Invoked as an example of the glory-seeking that drives men to great and violent deeds, and, in his assassination by a conspiracy of senators, as an instance of how the action of a few can be mistaken by a crowd for the action of the people as a whole.
